title: Is any man sick (James 5:13–16)
hookLine: call the priests to anoint the sick: the Church's root for anointing

lines: A SMALL METAL CASE OF OIL.
cards: Many parish priests carry a small metal case, about the size of a lipstick, with a screw-top lid. Inside is a bit of cotton soaked in olive oil, blessed by the bishop during Holy Week.
It rides in a coat pocket or a glove box for months. Then one night the phone rings: a hospital, a nursing home, a kitchen where someone's father has taken a turn.
The priest drives over, takes out the little case, and does something Christians have done since the first century. The instructions come from the end of the letter of James.

teach.b: James ends with three quick questions. Is anyone sad? Let him pray.

Is anyone cheerful? Let him sing. And then, in the Douay-Rheims: "Is any man sick among you? Let him bring in the priests of the church, and let them pray over him, anointing him with oil in the name of the Lord."
The sick person calls. Nobody is meant to suffer quietly in a back room so as not to be a bother.
James goes on: "And the prayer of faith shall save the sick man: and the Lord shall raise him up: and if he be in sins, they shall be forgiven him."
The Greek word for those priests is presbyteroi, elders, and the English word priest grows out of it.

teach.h: FROM LAST RITES TO ANOINTING OF THE SICK.
teach.b: The Church sees here the root of a sacrament, the Anointing of the Sick.

teach.h: THE PRAYER OF FAITH SHALL SAVE THE SICK MAN.
teach.b: The Council of Trent taught that it was hinted at in Mark's Gospel, where the twelve anointed many sick people with oil, and made known by James.
For centuries it was mostly given at the very end of life and called Extreme Unction, the last anointing.
After the Second Vatican Council the Church stressed its older name and wider use: anyone seriously ill, someone facing major surgery, the frail elderly, and it can be received more than once.

The priest lays his hands on the person in silence, then anoints the forehead and the hands. The Church doesn't promise a cure. It speaks of strength, peace and courage, and of bodily healing too, if God wills it.
Saved and raised up can mean more than one thing.

how: In the sacrament of the Anointing of the Sick, a priest prays over a seriously ill or elderly person, lays hands on them in silence and anoints their forehead and hands with oil blessed by the bishop; families can ask their parish or a hospital chaplain for it.

p: bring in the priests of the church
elders: root of the word priest

s: the Anointing of the Sick is only for people who are dying
since the Second Vatican Council the Church stresses it for anyone seriously ill, before major surgery, or frail with age.
the anointing can be received more than once
someone can receive it again in a new illness, or if the same illness grows worse.
the Church promises the anointing will cure the body
it speaks of strength, peace and courage, and of bodily healing if God wills it.

games.q: you're sick, and you belong to the church James is writing to. you don't want to be a bother. what does James tell you to do?
o: suffer quietly and wait to get better.
call in the priests of the church to pray over you and anoint you.
travel to wherever the apostles are.
games.why: James puts the first move in the sick person's hands: let him bring in the priests. nobody is meant to suffer alone in a back room.

practice: Bring to mind one person who is ill right now, at home, in the hospital, or carrying something no one can see. If it feels right, imagine your hand resting gently on their shoulder.
If you pray, pray for them by name; if not, stay with them in your thoughts and wish them strength and peace.

wordCard.voice: Presbyteroi, elders. James five: call the elders of the church to pray over the sick and anoint them with oil. Today's word.

orig.note: Greek: elders (James 5:14). the English word priest comes from it, through Latin presbyter.

carryVoice: Your line: the prayer of faith. The sick person calls, and the elders come. That's day six hundred seven.
